🚨 AI Agents don't just need better prompts. They need CONTRACTS.
We spend a lot of time improving:
🧠 Reasoning
📝 Prompts
🔧 Tool Calling
💾 Memory
🤖 Multi-Agent Orchestration
But production systems eventually hit a different problem:
What exactly is each agent allowed—and expected—to do?
If Agent A sends something to Agent B, hoping they'll “figure it out,” we've created another distributed system with an undocumented API. 😅
Production Agentic AI needs explicit Agent Contracts:
✅ Input / Output Schemas
✅ Structured Responses
✅ Tool Permissions
✅ Authentication & Authorization
✅ Timeout & Retry Policies
✅ Confidence Thresholds
✅ Error Handling
✅ State Transitions
✅ Human Escalation Rules
✅ Audit & Traceability
Instead of:
Agent A → “Research this” → Agent B
Think:
Agent A → Typed Task → Validated Output → Agent B
And if the contract is violated?
Fail predictably. Don't improvise silently.
As AI systems become more distributed, agent communication starts looking surprisingly familiar:
APIs + Events + State Machines + Policies + Observability
The future of Agentic AI won't only be about smarter agents.
It will be about well-engineered systems of agents.
💬 Question for the AI community:
What's MOST important in an Agent Contract?
A) Structured Input / Output
B) Permissions & Security
C) Failure / Retry Behavior
D) All of the above
Drop your choice—and how you're designing agent boundaries—below. 👇

Illinois Vs. Ohio AI Legislation
Contrasts by State – down to districts (Yikes!)
 
Illinois and Ohio are carving out vastly different regulatory paths for Artificial Intelligence (AI).
 
While Illinois enforces rigorous, mandatory guardrails across the private sector.
Ohio favors targeted, state-guided adoption and sector-specific governance.
 
Illinois: Comprehensive, High-Stakes AI Guardrails
 
Illinois has established itself as one of the nation's most aggressive states in regulating commercial and workplace AI usage:
 
Frontier Model Governance (AISMA / SB 315): AI Safety Measures Act subjects large developers (over $500M) to strict transparency rules, mandatory 72-hour incident reporting, and a first-in-the-nation req. for annual independent third-party audits.
 
Workplace Anti-Discrimination (HB 3773): Amends the Illinois Human Rights Act to make it a civil rights violation for employers to use AI tools that cause discriminatory impact in hiring, promotions, or discipline, requiring explicit employee notice.
 
Digital Likeness & Voice Protection (HB 4762): Restricts non-consensual digital replicas of voice and likeness in commercial contracts, establishing strong intellectual property (IP) protections for creators and workers.
 
Sector-Specific Restrictions: Prohibits AI from overriding licensed mental health professionals (HB 1806) or assigning scores in teacher evaluation reviews.
 
Ohio: Pragmatic Adoption and Educational Policy
 
Ohio focuses on structured framework building, public sector alignment, and localized governance rather than strict state-wide private corporate mandates:
 
Mandatory School District AI Policies (HB 96): Mandates that the Ohio Dept. of Edu. establish a model AI policy, requiring all public, charter, and STEM school districts to formally adopt AI usage and vendor evaluation policies by July 2026.
 
Statewide Strategic Framework (InnovateOhio): Ohio mandates data privacy, ethical tool evaluation, and vendor accountability across state-funded institutions.
 
Legal Personhood & Code Definitions (In-Motion / HB 469): Focuses foundational, e.g., AI sys. do not hold legal personhood or civil rights.
 
Vendor Procurement Standards: Directs gov’t. agencies and edu boards to implement formal vetting processes for third-party AI software before deployed.
 
Key Takeaway for Businesses
 
Orgs. operating in Illinois face substantial liability, civil rights oversight, & mandatory audit obligations if deploying high-risk or large-scale AI models.
 
In contrast, entities operating in Ohio must focus on public sector procure compliance, edu data stds., & navigating decentralized district-by-district policies.

Over the last couple of weeks I've spoken with CROs at several AI inference and model companies. 

Different businesses, but the same conversation kept coming up.

As inference matures, the sales profile they need is changing.

Early on, the job was getting a technical team to try the product. Now the buyer is often a platform or ML engineering leader who cares about latency, reliability and cost at scale, and the deals are getting bigger and more complex. 

That's created a gap. 

Traditional enterprise AEs can run a complex cycle but struggle to hold their own in a technical conversation. Technically fluent sellers from developer led companies often haven't closed large, multi stakeholder deals. 

The people who can do both are rare, and everyone is chasing the same small pool. 

So teams are restructuring around it:
→ Pairing AEs much more tightly with sales engineers or forward deployed engineers.
→ Hiring AEs who can grow usage after the contract is signed, not just close it.
→ Separating the early stage, developer led motion from the enterprise motion. 

If you're hiring for this profile right now, what's your biggest bottleneck?

As a specialist in Agency Recruitment Recruitment (!), I find myself sharing some daily nuggets to the Talent Acquisition folks out there who may be considering a change, or are finding it longer free space between each FTC or Perm role.

Ive confirmed my own sense of what was happening out there over the last couple of years by chatting to people who have followed some of this advice after chatting to me or simply by following their own gut instinct  👇 

1) Competition is fierce yes, but seeing 200+ applicants on an advertised role does not mean they are quality. Apply anyway, at best you get an interview, at worst you've left a digital footprint for the next role

2) Be your own agent! Budgets are tight - but there is work in the weeds where businesses must wonder  🧐  does someone like you exist. Connect to your sector, connect with CPOs and Heads of TA and offer up your CV on a golden platter. (Being open to a Contract and being agency-fee free, makes you an easier consideration)

3) Look to Competitor brands - if you've worked in ABC Ltd in FMCG, XYZ Ltd in FMCG would love your intel. Plonk your CV in their laps (with appropriate research done)

4) If you've ended up in Consultancy/Self Employed, very often the C Level hiring is where the gap is. A fully fledged and scaled TA team still only has 1 or 2 people seasoned enough to carry off the Exec Hiring (and they still have a full function or 3 to manage who don't feed up the food chain to help in this area) -

 Does it improve the talent pooling, high touch engagement and assessment and or onboarding of the C and D level hires to have a specialist service in this space. At worst, they may not have the budget for it,  at best you might bag yourself a new client/candidate/mandate

5) Your network needs you, and the stigma is well and truly passed for the green banner on your LinkedIn mugshot. Read Point 2 again  👆 

Ask where your skills might be needed / are there gaps that your skills can solve?

If TA teams have been whittled down to a shimmy of what they once were...this is exactly why projects / programs don't launch  🚀  ❌ and it might take a few disastrous campus recruitment days or an empty inbox on the old 'returnship' campaign to come around to extra hands needed to keep candidate flow or stem the bleed

No doubt some Big Corps are leaning heavily on the magic AI button to heal all wounds but meanwhile - you have your CV written up to fix todays pain points across Grad hiring, high attrition areas, hard to find skills, lack of process for international hiring, DEI hiring, or even just the basics around a good clear robust process thats transparent and repeatable for any SME - bingo!

Ive had 3 indirect placements happen just like this - returning to a previous client and saying  🤩  🤙  'Hey' - look what I can do if you ever have a need' = 1 internal conversation = 1 interview = Job Created for Lone Specialist Individual 

Good luck!

Work, Pay and AI: 
Who Gets the Gains?

A well-known chart from 2011 shows a turning point in the US economy. From 1947 to 1979, productivity rose 119%, and pay rose almost as much. Compensation went up 100% and wages 72%. From 1979 to 2009, productivity rose another 80%, but compensation grew only 8% and wages only 7%. Workers produced more and got almost nothing extra. The gains went mainly to the people who own companies and capital. Now AI may be the biggest productivity jump since electricity, so the question is who will benefit this time.

More people than ever have a degree. In the EU, 27% of young adults had one in 2005. In 2025 it was 45%. A degree still pays off. In 2025, 87% of recent graduates with a degree had a job, against 77% of those with only a secondary education. Graduates also earn about 54% more on average across wealthy countries. But a degree does not fix every gap. Women hold more degrees than men, 50.5% against 39.3%, yet women still earned 11% less per hour in 2024.

The first job is also getting harder to find. AI can already do many beginner tasks. In the US, employment of 22 to 25-year-olds fell 13% in the jobs most exposed to AI. In the UK, graduate hiring fell 8% in 2024/25. Higher costs and low business confidence play a part too, so AI is not the only reason. The logic is simple. A degree proves that you know things, and AI knows many of those things as well. Judgement, practical skill and ownership are harder to copy.

What happens next is open. The World Economic Forum expects 170 million new jobs and 92 million lost jobs worldwide by 2030. Three paths are possible. In the first, things stay roughly the same: degrees still pay, but starting a career is harder. In the second, the old pattern repeats, and owners and people with advanced degrees take most of the gains. In the third, the gains are shared through profit-sharing, like the 2026 IG Metall demand, and through pay transparency rules. The evidence shows the second path is a real risk, but it is not certain.

People can respond by using AI to build skills and judgement, and by trying to own something, such as shares, a product or a project. Employers can keep jobs open for beginners, publish pay data and set fair rules for sharing the gains from AI. Governments can enforce pay transparency and limit short-term contracts.

This text has limits. The chart ends in 2009 and covers US workers in non-management jobs. I found no data that compares Europe in 1995 or 1996 with 2026. The job forecasts are employer expectations, not facts. The gender pay gap does not adjust for working hours or job type.

Letter from America  📨 – much has changed, and it makes perfect sense for the US although not something that I've seen before. Some observations from the RICE energy technology venture fair in Houston and more....

🧲   The spectra of the new economic (or worse) cold war drives entrepreneurs and investors into critical mineral recovery, onshore electronics, dual use and cyber innovation. A level of resilience building (or insecurity) that I’ve not experienced in the US before. 

🏦 The higher cost of capital, and the drag effect of this in our sector including venture debt, project and acquisition finance, is only going to increase with cash demands from government and tech industrial expansion.  

🖥️ Techs disinterest in the volatility of its energy fuel source, the inefficiency of its power conversion and inflated capital costs confronts a utility industry that operates on system marginal pricing. Should these islands connect to the grid, they will be out of merit and held afloat only by the strength of the offtake contract. 

⛽  Wartime elevated oil prices aren’t leading to an expansion of US drilling but a contraction in hiring; the solution to high prices is no longer high prices. And as unconventional US oil resources mature, there will be a return to international exploration and innovation around enhanced oil recovery in shale.  

🚧 Just when the oil and gas industry profits from removing years of LNG export restrictions, it faces the prospect of a diesel export ban. Making it harder to argue in Tokyo or Brussels that the US is a more reliable partner than exports of solar panels and batteries from China. 

“So what?” for us in venture…. Industrial priorities, and for decision makers therein, are being reshaped by geopolitical shifts between regions, step-changing AI and climate tech, that are both outside of their control and changing at a rate not seen before.  

If we are to be useful, we need to pair VC investment success to industrial prosperity, through being as open as we can to prioritizing external innovation.

In 2018, Amazon scrapped an AI recruiting tool after discovering it had taught itself to downgrade CVs from women.

Eight years on, the BBC has spoken to more than 60 women aged 40 to 65, many with decades of senior experience, who are sending out applications and hearing almost nothing back. Several suspect automated screening is part of the reason. One described "Botoxing" her CV, stripping out anything that gave away her age.

https://lnkd.in/e2z8rpfM

Nobody can prove AI caused any individual rejection, and that's exactly the problem. Most candidates have no idea how they're being assessed, and many employers don't fully understand the tools they've bought either.

Running a temp and contract desk, I see the other side of this every day. Some of the strongest people we place are the ones whose CVs don't fit a neat pattern: career breaks, sector moves, raw material that can grow and develop. Those are exactly the profiles a filter trained on past hires is likely to miss.

AI has a real place in recruitment. But at VWA, we don't use it for CV screening, instead we have a fantastic Research Team who actually look at CVs, giving it a human touch. Instead, we use AI to help us find great people faster, not quietly deciding who never gets seen. 

If you want to hear more about our recruiting methods, including how we did a full graduate scheme programme this year, please reach out to myself or another team member, either directly or via recruit@vwa.com.

Als CRM Marketeer zorg jij dat Coolblue-klanten op het juiste moment een energiecontract aangeboden krijgen. Tegelijkertijd kijk je net zo goed naar de miljoenen Coolblue-klanten die nog geen energiecontract hebben. Je bedenkt hoe we energie zichtbaarder maken op Coolblue.nl: op productpaginas, in de bestelbevestiging en op de thankyou-page. Tussendoor schakel je de hele dag met het commerciële team om je heen. Met onze pricing specialist bespreek je welke tarief actie je het beste kunt uitlichten voor onze huidige klanten. Met de owner van Bespaardeals stem je af dat je een exclusieve korting wilt geven op een Sonos speaker. En met ons telesales team werk je het nauwst samen, want jouw campagnes leveren direct de leads op die zij aan de telefoon omzetten in contracten. After a great few months at Copper, I’ve found myself with an unexpected opportunity to think about what I want to do next.

Following a wider restructure, my role has been made redundant — so I’m officially back on the market.

And actually, I’m pretty excited about it.

I’m looking for a role where I can combine the things I enjoy most: Salesforce, integrations, automation, AI and solving real business problems.

I’ve always been slightly obsessed with the question:

“Why are we doing it this way?”

Sometimes the answer is “because that’s the best way.”
Quite often, it’s “because nobody has had time to find a better way.”

That’s what draws me to automation and process improvement.

More recently, I’ve been using AI — particularly Claude — almost like another member of the team. Not simply to write code, but to explore problems, challenge ideas, accelerate research and help work out what a better solution might look like.

I’m particularly interested in using AI and automation to remove the parts of work that never really needed a person in the first place — giving people more time to do the things that actually benefit from being human.

At Copper, I worked across third-party integrations, Salesforce automation, CI/CD and solutions supporting Revenue Operations, Relationship Management, Onboarding and KYC teams. Before that, I progressed into a senior technology role at REACT Disaster Response.

Alongside my technology career, I’ve continued building my career as a self-employed musician — which has taught me plenty about figuring things out, adapting quickly and making things happen without waiting for someone else to do it.

So I’m now open to:
🔹 Salesforce Developer / Salesforce Engineer roles
🔹 Integration & Automation roles
🔹 Salesforce Architecture opportunities
🔹 Contract or permanent positions

Last night I went to a funeral for the billable hour (aka "Bill"). In an actual church.

It was Falcon's launch at Sint-Coleta in Ghent, and it confirmed something I've believed for a while: the most interesting AI companies won't be tools. They'll be AI-native services firms.

In legal, that's not another AI product lawyers buy to work a bit faster, but a firm that sells the outcome: NDAs, DPAs and commercial contracts reviewed and signed off by a real lawyer, for a flat fee. The client gets the work back faster and at a predictable price. Internally you run lean on AI, which gets you margins traditional services firms can't reach.

Y Combinator has been making this case for a while: rebuild services businesses from scratch with AI at the core, sell the result, and keep humans where judgment and liability actually sit.

I spent the evening talking with other founders in this space, including the team at Duely, who are building an AI-native services firm for legal M&A: data rooms, legal DD, gap analysis, SPAs. Inspiring to hear how they're rethinking the business model from the ground up.

Running LexGO, the part I'm most curious about is hiring. A firm that sells outcomes needs a different team than one that sells hours. I'll be watching that closely.

Congrats to the Falcon team on the launch!

Last week, I asked what percentage of people you thought would be open to a career move if the right opportunity came along. 

83 of you voted. Half said 90%+

I promised you the real data so I went back through my own records. Every message since 2024 where I approached someone about a role. Of the people who gave me a clear answer, 74% said yes, lets talk. 26% said no. Roughly 3 in 4 we're open to a move for the right opportunity. So the poll results were a little off but not far!

The part employers should pay attention to is the reasons for the No. Almost nobody said I'm never moving. It was nearly always a reason with a date on it: 
 👉 I've only just joined 
 👉 I've got a bonus landing at the end of Q 
 👉 My visa is tied to my current employer 
 👉 The current contract I'm on is too good to leave right now 
 👉 Now isn't the right time to move for personal reasons

Ask most of those people again in a few months and plenty would be a yes. 

If you're hiring and telling yourself the good people aren't on the market, they are. They just need a better reason to move or be contacted at the right time. If you're finding the right people wont even pick up the phone, drop me a message.

DuoSkill ships four AI features in one platform — ATS resume optimization, AI interview prep, Greenhouse integration, and automated hiring workflows — per duoskill.com. That's a lot of surface area for a tester to take on faith.

The parser returns a name, the simulator plays audio, the form submits. Green check.

But the model underneath is doing the actual work, and nobody wrote a test for it. Here's how I'd cover it.

→ Resume parser fidelity: feed the same candidate across .pdf, .docx, and a scanned image. If the ATS score shifts between formats, that's not a UI bug — that's a hiring decision changing silently.

→ Interview simulator logic: don't just confirm the audio plays. Run a candidate who gives a deliberately weak answer, then a strong one.

The scoring has to move. → Cross-browser and device coverage: a Greenhouse webhook that fires twice in Safari and once in Chrome isn't a browser quirk.

It's a duplicate candidate in someone's pipeline. → Negative paths: empty resume, 10-page resume, resume with only emojis.

AI features fail in stranger ways than CRUD apps. Write those cases before the user finds them.

→ End-to-end flows: job seeker uploads resume, gets parsed, schedules mock interview, completes it, lands in Greenhouse. Walk the whole loop from both sides.

Treat the AI feature like a production system with its own contract. Inputs in, outputs out, edge cases documented.

If your QA team is still signing off on AI features with a happy-path screenshot, the next defect report is going to come from a recruiter, not a tester. Try it now at duoskill.com — poke at the parser and the simulator before you ship your own.

More than a third of UK organisations say technology skills gaps have cost them at least £380,000 in the past year. Among the largest firms, those turning over £73 million or more, that rises to 57%, with 15% reporting costs of £760,000 or higher.

That's from Pluralsight's annual Tech Skills Report, published this week, surveying 500 UK tech executives, IT professionals, and learning and development leaders.

The number isn't abstract. It's showing up as 40% of organisations unexpectedly outsourcing or hiring externally for project work they thought they could deliver in-house. 39% failing to deliver key projects. 30% reporting budget overruns. 27% losing a client or contract outright. Each of those is a moment where someone discovered, after the fact, that the capability they assumed existed inside the organisation didn't.

Here's the detail that doesn't fit the usual story. 85% of these organisations hired the same number of junior tech staff this year or more. This isn't a pipeline that's run dry at the recruitment stage. And yet 88% say they're worried they don't have enough junior talent coming through to close the skills gaps AI itself can't solve.

So people are coming in. The worry is about what happens to them once they're inside. 46% of technology workers say they struggle to find time for training. 28% of L&D leaders cite a lack of support from leadership as a barrier to upskilling. 53% of senior leaders admit they're unsure how to solve their own skills gaps.

Pluralsight frames this as a cycle: leaders recognise the need for new capability, employees lack the time and organisational backing to build it. That's accurate, but it understates what's actually happening underneath. An organisation can hire well, invest in tools, 94% have invested in AI tools for at least some staff, and still have no reliable picture of what its people can do a year after they walk through the door. 

The gap isn't at the hiring stage. It's in the complete absence of any ongoing, verified record of what capability actually developed, stalled, or quietly went unused.

Matthew Lloyd Davies, Pluralsight's principal security author, makes the point sharply in the context of cybersecurity specifically: skills gaps are costly because they lengthen the window before a problem is caught, and cost scales with that window staying open. 

The same logic applies more broadly. The longer an organisation goes without actually knowing what its workforce can do, the more expensive the eventual discovery becomes. £380,000 is what it costs to find out the hard way, through a failed project or a lost client. Knowing earlier isn't a training problem. It's a visibility problem.

If your organisation is investing in junior hiring and in training, what's actually tracking whether either one is closing the gap?

Your AI resume scorer told you a candidate is "strong" — but what if it produced no output, and you never knew?

When you ask an LLM to score a resume, you're relying on a contract: 200 OK + valid JSON. You assume that means "I evaluated this candidate." But the contract guarantees only that the response was well-formed.

An LLM can return HTTP 200, valid JSON, and zero output tokens — all three at once. No reasoning, no scores, no signal. Your hiring pipeline saw 200 and treated it as a real evaluation.

Why does this happen? Context limits, model confusion, prompt fatigue in batch jobs. The response looks right. The actual judgment never occurred.

The cost is silent: a strong candidate slides into the "maybe later" pile. You never know you missed them. They take a different offer.

This failure can't be caught by asking "did the model error?" It succeeded at returning a response while failing at the actual task.

When you're automating hiring, you need visibility into whether the AI step actually ran — not just whether the API call returned 200. Silent failures mean candidates scored wrong without anyone knowing. It's not a broken workflow — it's a hire you never made.

Give it a year and most CVs will say proficient with Claude.

Think about what that does to you if you're the one hiring.

Forty applications. 

Most of them make the claim. 

You can't test it in an interview without handing someone a laptop and an hour you haven't got.

So the claim stops meaning much. 

Everyone making it may well be telling the truth. 

There is still nothing in it that separates one person from another.

A certificate doesn't make someone good. 

It sets a floor. 

It says this person sat a proctored exam, closed book, no AI in the room, and scored above the line.

That's all it says. 

It also happens to be enough to turn forty CVs into two piles.

Right now almost nobody is claiming it. 

We looked at 132 UK Claude Code contract roles over twelve months and certification came up zero times. 

AWS certification came up three.

That is what an empty field looks like, and empty fields fill.

I am a strong proponent of structured onboarding, whether the hire is senior or junior. Onboarding is broader than induction. Clear expectations, access, manager alignment and deliberate integration help people get traction faster. Ambiguity is not autonomy, and clarity does not require every intervention to be selected in advance.

A draft 30/60/90 plan I was reviewing made that tension visible. In the first 30 days, the new executive was expected to understand the customer and commercial issues, establish a baseline, review the roadmap and diagnose the constraints. The same plan also required two AI-enabled workflows to be live.

That expectation may be right. The risk appears when the whole performance contract is read together: the executive is still expected to establish where performance is constrained, yet one intervention has already been prescribed as evidence of success.

The cost can be senior time, capacity and organisational attention committed before there is enough room to establish whether that intervention addresses the right constraint, at the right point and at the right time.

This is where the bookends help. At one end is the business objective this appointment is meant to advance and why it matters now. At the other is the business outcome and value that would show the appointment is working.

What sits between them should not be vague, but neither should it be over-prescribed. The executive still has to establish where movement is being lost, what deserves priority, which intervention fits the condition and what needs to move downstream.

The more precisely we prescribe the middle, the less room remains for the senior capability we paid for.

The expectation for early movement stays. What changes is what Day 30 has to prove: can the executive connect the business objective to the constraint, the intervention chosen, the downstream movement expected and the business outcome it is meant to influence?

If the prescribed intervention survives that test, it stays. If it does not, changing course early is part of the return on hiring senior capability.

That is one practical use of the Business Constraint™ Scan around a senior appointment: testing whether the mandate, intervention and intended business result belong on the same route before the success criteria harden around one answer.

📊 Procurement data is becoming a strategic asset

Procurement organisations have access to something many companies underestimate: a remarkably detailed view of how the business actually spends money — categories, suppliers, contracts, business units, geographies, payment terms, volumes, dependencies, and increasingly risk indicators.

This creates an opportunity. Spend analysis can evolve from reporting what happened to helping executives understand what may happen next: where is the business overly dependent on one supplier, where are contracts expiring, where is spend fragmented, where are price increases hidden inside contract renewals, where is supplier concentration becoming a business risk.

AI can accelerate parts of this analysis. But AI doesn't solve poor data. If supplier identities are fragmented, categories inconsistent and contracts disconnected from transactions, the smartest AI model will simply produce faster answers from imperfect information. That's why the next Procurement transformation isn't primarily an AI project. It's a data architecture project — and then an AI project.

This distinction matters enormously when hiring Procurement technology leaders. The strongest profiles understand three worlds simultaneously: Procurement, technology, and data. That combination is still relatively rare.
